 Live FAA ground stop latest updates: Controllers’ union chief says communications with some planes were disrupted; cancellations top 5,000; Duffy blames L3Harris
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed contractor L3Harris but said officials haven’t determined whether the outage was caused by the company’s error or a faulty router. L3Harris says it’s supporting the FAA’s investigation.
 Kate Murphy , Andrew Romano , Jack Brewster Updated Sat, November 14, 2026 at 8:40 PM UTC Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, and Rebecca Gay, FAA Acting Chief Technology Officer, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner) (AP Photo/Tom Brenner) Airlines canceled thousands more flights Saturday as they recovered from Friday's nationwide ground stop, but the FAA said schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.
 More than 5,000 U.S. flights had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware , already past the top of the 4,000 to 5,000 that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford predicted. Flight-tracking app Flighty said the outage has now caused more cancellations than the 2024 CrowdStrike software failure. "I do think the worst is behind us," Bedford said, and he apologized to travelers.
 The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. About 12,000 flights couldn't be completed, Bedford said.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began while L3Harris Technologies, which runs the network, was doing routine work to switch lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. A router involved in the work flooded the rest of the system, disrupting communications with airplanes and radar. Duffy said officials are working to determine "whether we had incompetence" by the contractor or a faulty router. "Until I can build" a new network, he said, "I'm stuck with L3Harris." Bedford said the review will determine whether the router was installed or configured incorrectly, or was simply defective.
 In a statement to Yahoo News, L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation" and "takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." The company did not address Duffy's criticism or say what went wrong.
 Asked why the work was done on a Friday afternoon, Duffy said work at small, remote sites is done during the day because it isn't expected to affect the wider system. "There'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work," he said. Bedford said maintenance on the network is logged on paper, so officials had to search through paper records to figure out who was working where.
 Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told Yahoo News that communications with some planes were disrupted during the outage and that controllers moved flights to working frequencies. Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, he said, "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky."
 Advertisement Advertisement The network's problems aren't new. A 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review called it obsolete, CBS News reported . In 2009, a technician for L3Harris' predecessor, Harris Corp., misconfigured a router while moving the network to fiber, disrupting 129 air traffic facilities, according to a Transportation Department inspector general review .
 Duffy is pressing Congress for more money to replace the system. President Trump has asked for $30 billion and Duffy has said he wants $50 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion Congress approved last year. Bedford said the router swap was routine maintenance, not part of that modernization effort.
 New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign Saturday. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation .
 Travelers whose flights were canceled are owed a refund if they choose not to fly, and most major airlines are offering travel waivers. Airlines' promises of hotels and meals generally cover only disruptions within their control, which doesn't include an FAA ground stop.
 Live 29 updates Sat, Nov 14, 2026 08:22 PM UTC Jack Brewster Controllers' union chief says communications with some planes were disrupted during outage
 National Air Traffic Controllers Association President Nick Daniels speaks during a news conference at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on September 28, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
 (Andrew Harnik via Getty Images) The head of the air traffic controllers' union told Yahoo News in a phone interview Saturday that communications with some planes were disrupted during Friday's outage. Controllers across the country had to scramble to keep flights moving safely, he said.
 "We had controllers working with one another across the United States to see whose frequencies were working, whose radar was working," said Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association. Controllers checked whether they could hand off planes to one another if their own frequencies went down, he said.
 Daniels said he hadn't reviewed the FAA's safety data. But asked what controllers had told him, he said, "We know we didn't have communications with airplanes, or that we were switching airplanes to different frequencies because their communications were being disrupted." Controllers "ensured the safety of every aircraft," he said.
 FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a news conference earlier Saturday that "no facilities went dark," but acknowledged reports of "certain frequencies that were going in and out."
 Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, Daniels said it depends on the risk. "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky," he said. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that work at small, remote sites is routinely done during the day and that the practice will be reevaluated.
 Daniels said such failures often happen when the FAA's required safety reviews before maintenance aren't followed. He said he didn't know whether that happened Friday.
 Daniels wouldn't say whether Duffy was right to blame contractor L3Harris. "I don't think blame changes anything. Action changes things," Daniels said. He said the union has warned for more than a decade that the system is failing, noting that the FAA still uses floppy disks in some cases to update computers.
 Daniels said any new money for the air traffic control system should also go toward controllers' pay and working conditions. He said he hasn't spoken with Duffy since the outage, but that Duffy "already knows" the union's position. "We're going to continue working on that with this administration," he said.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 07:48 PM UTC Jack Brewster Saturday cancellations top 5,000, passing FAA’s forecast
 More than 5,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware . FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had predicted 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations for the day.
 American has canceled the most flights, 892, followed by Delta (734), United (733) and Southwest (540). JetBlue has canceled 43% of its schedule.
 The air traffic control system itself appears to be running near normal, and no airports had ground stops in effect Saturday afternoon. The problem now is getting planes and crews back where they're supposed to be.
 Sunday looks better so far. About 130 U.S. flights scheduled for Sunday had been canceled as of Saturday afternoon.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 07:27 PM UTC Jack Brewster L3Harris says it's supporting the FAA investigation, doesn't address Duffy's criticism
 L3Harris Technologies said Saturday it is supporting the FAA's investigation into Friday's outage. Earlier that day, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy publicly questioned whether the company's "incompetence" caused the outage.
 "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," an L3Harris spokesperson said in a statement to Yahoo News. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
 The company said that, "together with its telco partners and the FAA," it has completed more than 70% of the planned switch from copper wire to fiber optic lines. The statement doesn't say what caused the outage or respond to Duffy's suggestion of contractor error.
 Asked whether L3Harris employees or a partner company did Friday's work, and whether the company disputes Duffy's suggestion of contractor error, a spokesperson said the company had nothing to offer beyond its statement.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 06:33 PM UTC Jack Brewster American gives commuting crews confirmed seats to speed recovery
 Airlines' biggest challenge Saturday is getting pilots and flight attendants to the planes they're scheduled to fly.
 American Airlines is giving crew members who commute to work confirmed seats on Saturday, instead of the usual standby travel, CNN reported . The memo also tells crews to wait for updated schedules before booking a flight to work, "to help ensure the flight you intend to commute on is fully crewed and operating as scheduled."
 Many crews ended Friday night far from where they were supposed to be. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that's the main reason airlines are still canceling flights Saturday.
 Advertisement Advertisement 
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 05:36 PM UTC Jack Brewster What we still don’t know about the outage
 Officials explained the basics of Friday's outage on Saturday, but several key questions remain unanswered:
 Was it the router or the installer? Officials don't know yet whether the router installed at the remote site was defective, or whether L3Harris installed or configured it incorrectly. Duffy said they'll share the findings when the review is done.
 Where was the site? Officials described it only as "a very remote location" and haven't named it.
 Why didn't anyone catch it sooner? It took about 45 minutes to trace the problem. Bedford said that's partly because maintenance is logged on paper.
 Will there be consequences for L3Harris? Duffy said "we're going to hold people accountable" but didn't say how. L3Harris has not responded to Yahoo News' request for comment.
 Could it happen again? Bedford said the network "will continue to break until we replace it." Officials haven't said whether daytime maintenance will stop before Thanksgiving.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:54 PM UTC Jack Brewster Key takeaways from the FAA briefing on the ground stop
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford and FAA Chief Technology Officer Rebecca Guy briefed reporters Saturday on what caused Friday's nationwide ground stop. Here's what we learned:
 Duffy blamed contractor L3Harris: He said a router installed during L3Harris' work at a remote site flooded the network. Officials are still checking "whether we had incompetence" or a faulty router. "We're going to hold people accountable," Duffy said.
 The FAA shut off the suspect routers: Guy said the FAA disabled the problem function on the roughly 60 routers of the same type in use nationwide, and is doing more testing with L3Harris.
 It wasn't a cyberattack or AI: Bedford said there's "zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related."
 Flights should be back to normal by Sunday night. Bedford expects 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations Saturday and full recovery by the close of business Sunday. He apologized to travelers.
 The FAA will rethink daytime maintenance. Work at small sites is done during the day, Duffy said. "There'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work."
 The network will keep failing until it's replaced, Bedford said: "Let's not kid ourselves; it will continue to break until we replace it." All facilities rely on one network, he said, and "there's no backup to the backup."
 Duffy will send Congress a new funding request Monday: Bedford said finishing the modernization will take about $10.1 billion more. Duffy wants more than that for towers, runways and other upgrades.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:45 PM UTC Jack Brewster Duffy: ‘This is a safe system’
 Duffy closed the briefing by trying to reassure travelers.
 "I fly all the time. My kids fly. My wife flies. This is a safe system, evidenced by what happened yesterday," he said. "We will keep you on the ground. You won't get to your destination if we think you can't get there safely."
 Duffy said his first full day on the job was the day of the January 2025 midair collision near Reagan National Airport, which killed 67 people. "That's not an experience that I ever want to have again," he said.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:43 PM UTC Jack Brewster Lawmakers in both parties promise review
 Lawmakers from both parties say Congress will investigate what caused Friday's ground stop.
 Rep. Sam Graves of Missouri, the Republican chair of the House Transportation Committee, and Rep. Rick Larsen of Washington, the panel's top Democrat, said in a joint statement Friday that the communication failures were "concerning" and that their committee will "thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop."
 Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, said the committee will review the technology problems behind the outage. The committee's Republicans said in a post on X that the outage highlights the need to modernize air traffic control centers.
 Some Democrats went further. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called for Duffy to resign Saturday. Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate aviation subcommittee, pushed back on Duffy blaming Congress. "You've literally controlled Congress for the past two years," she wrote on X .
 FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday he expects "a very transparent hearing" on what happened.
 Advertisement Advertisement 
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:40 PM UTC Jack Brewster FAA chief warns old network ‘will continue to break’ until replaced
 Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, with Rebecca Gay, FAA Acting Chief Technology Officer, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner)
 (AP Photo/Tom Brenner) FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that the telecommunications network behind Friday's outage has been flagged as a weakness for years and will keep failing until it's replaced.
 "Every agency within the government for better than two decades has flagged this FTI system as a critical weakness," Bedford said, calling it "one of the worst kept secrets in government." He added, "Let's not kid ourselves; it will continue to break until we replace it."
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:29 PM UTC Jack Brewster What is FTI, the network that failed?
 The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, or FTI, is the private network that connects air traffic control centers, towers and radar sites across the country. It carries controllers' voice communications with pilots and the radar data they use to track planes.
 L3Harris has run the network since 2002, under a contract its predecessor, Harris Corp., won that year. It connects more than 4,000 FAA facilities and still relies partly on decades-old copper-wire technology, which the FAA is replacing with fiber.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:26 PM UTC Jack Brewster FAA chief says airlines are waiving restrictions, promising rebooking or ‘full refund’
 FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that airlines are "waiving all of their terms and conditions" for travelers affected by the ground stop.
 "Everyone will either be reaccommodated on a flight or they'll get a full refund," Bedford said. He urged travelers to "reach out to your air carriers directly."
 Individual airlines' published waivers vary, though. American's covers trips at 21 airports and requires changes by Saturday. Delta's covers travel through Sunday. Check your airline's travel alerts page for the exact terms.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:23 PM UTC Jack Brewster FAA chief says ‘no facilities went dark’ during outage
 Asked why backup systems didn't prevent the outage, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said, "No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully lost."
 He said the FAA's facilities have several backup channels, but they all run over a single telecommunications network. "We have one federal telephony infrastructure," Bedford said. "We don't have two, but one."
 Advertisement Advertisement 
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:22 PM UTC Jack Brewster What is L3Harris, the company at the center of the outage?
 Sam Mehta became CEO of L3Harris Technologies, which runs the FAA's telecommunications network, in August.
 (L3Harris Technologies) L3Harris Technologies is a defense contractor based in Melbourne, Florida, with about 45,000 employees and $21.9 billion in revenue last year. It's best known for military communications, space and missile systems.
 Its predecessor, Harris Corp., won the contract to build and run the FAA's telecommunications network in 2002.
 Sam Mehta became CEO in August, after the board ousted Christopher Kubasik for conduct that broke company rules, Reuters reported. That same month, the FAA picked AT&T to lead a replacement for the network, saying it "can no longer support" air traffic operations, Nextgov reported .
 L3Harris has not responded to Yahoo News' request for comment.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:18 PM UTC Jack Brewster Duffy says FAA will 'reevaluate' doing network work during the day
 Asked why the switch from copper to fiber was done at 3 p.m. on a Friday instead of overnight, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA does work at small, remote sites during the day because it isn't expected to affect the wider system.
 "It shouldn't have that kind of impact, which is what we saw yesterday," Duffy said. "So there'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work."
 Work at major facilities is done at night, he said. Some air traffic controllers had questioned the daytime timing, Anna Giaritelli posted on X Friday night.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:16 PM UTC Jack Brewster FAA chief says ‘zero evidence’ outage was tied to AI
 FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that officials have found "zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI related" in Friday's outage.
 "We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue," Bedford said. He said officials are still working out whether a piece of equipment was badly installed, misconfigured or simply defective.
 Questions about AI came up because the FAA began a nationwide rollout of a new $875 million AI tool, called SMART, this week to help controllers manage traffic. Its maker, Air Space Intelligence, said Friday the ground stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system."
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:15 PM UTC Jack Brewster FAA expects 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations today, full recovery by Sunday night
 US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy (R) speaks alongside FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford (L) during a press briefing at the Department of Transportation headquarters building in Washington, DC, on November 14, 2026. (Photo by Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)
 (AARON SCHWARTZ via Getty Images) FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that airlines will likely cancel 4,000 to 5,000 of the roughly 41,000 flights scheduled today. He said airlines expect their schedules to be fully back to normal "by the close of business on Sunday."
 "I do think the worst is behind us," Bedford said at a news conference. "But we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do."
 About 12,000 flights couldn't be completed Friday after the ground stop, Bedford said. Roughly 9,000 were commercial flights and 3,000 were private or general aviation flights. Many crews and planes ended the night out of position.
 Bedford also apologized. "Sincere apologies to the American traveling public," he said. "I'm sorry that we put you through this, but we did it for the right reasons."
 Advertisement Advertisement 
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:09 PM UTC Jack Brewster Duffy says Trump promised ‘every resource’ to fix air traffic control
 Duffy said President Trump told him in phone calls since the outage that he would back the FAA with whatever it needs.
 "He said, 'I will commit every resource of the federal government, whatever you need. I am going to give those resources to the FAA to make sure you guys can do this, do it fast, do it right,'" Duffy said.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:09 PM UTC Jack Brewster Duffy presses Congress for more money after outage
 Duffy used part of the briefing to press Congress again for more money to overhaul the air traffic control system.
 "I've been talking about this for almost two years, and I've been asking the Congress for money," he said. Congress gave the department "a partial payment" of $12.5 billion last year, he said.
 The network's problems aren't new. A 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review called it obsolete, CBS News reported . In 2009, a technician for L3Harris' predecessor, Harris Corp., misconfigured a router while moving the network to fiber, disrupting 129 air traffic facilities, according to a Transportation Department inspector general review .
 Republicans control both chambers of Congress until January, when Democrats take over after winning majorities in this month's midterm elections.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:04 PM UTC Jack Brewster Duffy says outage was not a cyberattack, describes router ‘flooding’ the system
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that officials don't believe Friday's outage was a cyberattack.
 "Did some foreign nation attack this network, and the answer to that is we don't believe so," Duffy said at a news conference. "Once we're able to isolate what was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online. So we don't believe this was cyber at all."
 Duffy said a router involved in the switch from copper wire to fiber "started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system." The system saw "over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds," he said. That disrupted communications with airplanes and radar.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 04:01 PM UTC Jack Brewster Duffy blames L3Harris contractor work, says officials are checking for ‘incompetence’
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, arrives for a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner)
 (AP Photo/Tom Brenner) Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that the outage began while L3Harris Technologies was switching telecommunications lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. He said officials are still trying to determine whether the cause was contractor error or faulty equipment.
 "Here's what we believe happened yesterday," Duffy said at a news conference at Transportation Department headquarters. He said a contractor was doing maintenance at "at least one" remote FAA location "to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they're bringing it over to fiber."
 That contractor is L3Harris, the FAA's "legacy provider" for more than 20 years, Duffy said. "L3Harris actually owns that network," he said.
 The work was needed because the copper line was so old it was being discontinued, Duffy said. "This is not complicated. It's pretty straightforward work," he said.
 Officials are working to determine "whether we had incompetence," Duffy said, meaning human error by the contractor, or a faulty router. "We haven't determined what the fault was," he said.
 L3Harris did not immediately respond to Yahoo News' request for comment.
